Exercise A

A Nation Divided

Read the text carefully, then answer the comprehension questions using the dropdown menus.

Reading Text

For more than two hundred years before the American Civil War, millions of enslaved African people had been forced to work on plantations in the southern United States. They had been taken from their homes in Africa, transported across the Atlantic in terrible conditions, and sold as property. By the middle of the 19th century, the economy of the South depended heavily on their unpaid labour.

The northern states, which had already abolished slavery, increasingly opposed the system. This deep disagreement finally split the country. When Abraham Lincoln, who was against the spread of slavery, was elected president in 1860, eleven southern states decided to leave the United States. The Civil War began in 1861.

The war lasted four long years and cost more lives than any other conflict in American history. In 1863, while the fighting continued, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared that enslaved people in the rebel states were now free. By the time the war ended in 1865, the northern states had won, and slavery was soon abolished throughout the country.

The end of slavery, however, was not the end of the struggle. Although they had gained their freedom, formerly enslaved people and their descendants would face discrimination for many generations to come.
